notes.summary: This chapter, as rationalised by NCERT, focuses on heredity: how variations accumulate during reproduction, Mendel's experiments with garden pea and the rules of inheritance (monohybrid and dihybrid crosses), how genes control traits, and sex determination. CBSE tests it through cross-based ratio and probability questions, assertion-reason items and case-based questions built on Mendel's experiments.
keyPoints: Variation: asexual reproduction gives only minor differences, caused by small inaccuracies in DNA copying; sexual reproduction combines DNA from two parents and produces much greater diversity. Variants suited to a changed environment survive better.

Mendel worked with garden pea, using contrasting visible characters such as round/wrinkled seeds, yellow/green seeds, tall/short plants and violet/white flowers. Each trait is controlled by two copies of a factor (gene), one inherited from each parent.

Monohybrid cross: TT (tall) × tt (short) → F₁ all Tt (tall). F₁ selfed (Tt × Tt) → F₂ phenotype 3 tall : 1 short; genotype 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. So only 1/4 of the F₂ plants are pure tall. No medium-height plants appear because the traits do not blend.

Dominant trait: expressed even with one copy (Tt shows tallness). Recessive trait: expressed only when both copies are recessive (tt). A trait hidden in F₁ reappears in F₂ because F₁ plants are heterozygous carriers.

Dihybrid cross: RRYY (round yellow) × rryy (wrinkled green) → F₁ RrYy, all round yellow. F₂ ratio 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green. The new combinations (round green, wrinkled yellow) show that the two traits are inherited independently. Example: out of 1600 F₂ plants, 3/16 × 1600 = 300 are round green.
Test cross: crossing an unknown tall plant with tt — all offspring tall means the parent is TT; a 1 : 1 ratio of tall and short means it is Tt.

Genes control traits through proteins: a gene is a section of DNA carrying information for one protein. NCERT example: plant height depends on the amount of a growth hormone, which depends on how efficient the enzyme making it is; a gene change that makes the enzyme less efficient gives less hormone and a shorter plant.

Germ cells carry only one set of chromosomes (one from each pair), so when two germ cells fuse the full number is restored. Humans have 23 pairs (46 chromosomes) in body cells and 23 in each gamete; this keeps the chromosome number constant across generations.

Sex determination: in some reptiles the incubation temperature of fertilised eggs decides the sex; snails can change sex. In humans, 22 pairs are autosomes and one pair is the sex chromosomes: females XX, males XY. The mother always gives an X; a sperm carrying X gives a girl and one carrying Y gives a boy, so every birth has an independent 1/2 chance of being a boy.
traps: Confusing the phenotypic ratio 3 : 1 with the genotypic ratio 1 : 2 : 1 — three-quarters of F₂ plants are tall, but only one-quarter are pure tall (TT).
Calling F₁ plants of a pure-breeding cross homozygous: they are heterozygous (Tt).
Thinking earlier children change the odds: the chance of a boy is 1/2 at every birth.
In 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, the 9 is the double-dominant class and the 1 is the double-recessive class; round green and wrinkled yellow are the 3 : 3 new combinations.
Deciding dominance from a single family: one cross is often consistent with either trait being dominant.
notes.examTip: For any cross, write the gametes and draw a quick Punnett square before choosing an option, and check whether the question asks for a phenotype or a genotype, and for a fraction of all offspring or of only one group.

questions.text: Which of the following produces the greatest diversity (variation) among offspring?
options: Binary fission in bacteria
Budding in yeast
Sexual reproduction
Vegetative propagation in potato
questions.explanation: In asexual methods such as binary fission, budding and vegetative propagation, offspring get DNA from a single parent and differ only slightly, due to small errors in DNA copying. In sexual reproduction, DNA from two different parents combines in the offspring. This generates much greater diversity, so the answer is sexual reproduction.

questions.text: In some reptiles, the sex of the offspring is determined by:
options: the temperature at which the fertilised eggs are kept
the X and Y chromosomes of the father
the diet of the mother before laying eggs
the number of eggs laid at a time
questions.explanation: NCERT explains that different species use different strategies for sex determination. In some reptiles, the temperature at which the fertilised eggs are incubated decides whether the offspring will be male or female. Snails can even change sex, while in humans sex is decided genetically by X and Y chromosomes. So in these reptiles, it is the incubation temperature.

questions.text: Mendel studied several pairs of contrasting characters in garden pea. Which of the following was NOT one of them?
options: Round vs wrinkled seeds
Tall vs short plants
Violet vs white flowers
Broad vs narrow leaves
questions.explanation: Mendel chose clearly contrasting visible characters in garden pea. His seven characters were seed shape, seed colour, flower colour, flower position, pod shape, pod colour and stem height. Round/wrinkled seeds, tall/short plants and violet/white flowers are among them. Leaf shape was not one of his characters, so the answer is broad vs narrow leaves.

questions.text: A pure tall (TT) pea plant is crossed with a pure short (tt) plant, and the F₁ plants are self-pollinated. What fraction of the F₂ plants will be pure tall (TT)?
questions.explanation: TT × tt gives F₁ plants that are all Tt. Selfing Tt × Tt gives the gametes T and t from each parent. The Punnett square gives TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1. Tall plants make up 3/4, but pure tall (TT) plants are only 1 out of 4, that is 1/4.

questions.text: A couple already has two daughters. What is the probability that their third child will be a son?
options: 1 (certain)
questions.explanation: The mother always contributes an X chromosome. Half of the father's sperms carry X and half carry Y. A sperm with Y gives a boy (XY) and one with X gives a girl (XX). Each conception is independent of earlier births, so the probability of a son is 1/2.

questions.text: A tall pea plant is crossed with a short pea plant (tt). Half of the offspring are tall and half are short. The genotype of the tall parent is:
options: Tt
TT
tt
It cannot be determined
questions.explanation: The short parent (tt) can give only t gametes. If the tall parent were TT, every offspring would be Tt and tall. Getting short (tt) offspring means the tall parent must also give t gametes, half the time. Tt × tt gives 1 Tt (tall) : 1 tt (short), which matches the result, so the tall parent is Tt.

questions.text: According to NCERT, how can a gene control the height of a plant?
options: The gene directly stretches the cells of the stem.
The gene decides the number of leaves, which alone fixes the height.
The gene itself is converted into a hormone that travels to the stem.
The gene carries information for an enzyme; the efficiency of this enzyme decides how much growth hormone is made, and hence the plant's height.
questions.explanation: A gene is a section of DNA that provides information for making one protein. Plant height depends on the amount of a particular plant hormone, and the amount made depends on the efficiency of the enzyme that produces it. An efficient enzyme gives more hormone and a tall plant, while a gene change that makes the enzyme less efficient gives less hormone and a short plant. So the gene acts through an enzyme that controls hormone production.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): When pure tall pea plants are crossed with pure short pea plants, no plants of medium height appear in the F₁ or F₂ generation.
Reason (R): Traits are inherited as separate units (genes) that do not blend, and the factor for tallness is dominant over that for shortness.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.explanation: Mendel found that all F₁ plants were tall and that F₂ plants were either tall or short in a 3 : 1 ratio, with no medium-height plants, so A is true. This happens because the factors for height are separate units that do not mix, and the tall factor masks the short one, so R is true. R is the reason no halfway height appears, so both are true and R correctly explains A.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Shortness, which is not seen in the F₁ generation of a cross between pure tall and pure short pea plants, reappears in the F₂ generation.
Reason (R): The F₁ plants are homozygous (TT) for tallness.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.explanation: In F₂, one-quarter of the plants are short, so the hidden trait does reappear and A is true. The F₁ plants are Tt, heterozygous, because they receive T from the tall parent and t from the short parent. That is exactly why selfing them can produce tt plants. Since R wrongly calls them TT, R is false. A is true, but R is false.

questions.text: Mendel crossed pea plants having round yellow seeds (RRYY) with plants having wrinkled green seeds (rryy). The F₁ plants were self-pollinated and 1600 F₂ plants were obtained. How many F₂ plants are expected to have round green seeds?
questions.explanation: The F₁ plants are RrYy, all round yellow. Because the two traits are inherited independently, the F₂ phenotypic ratio is 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green, out of 16. Round green = 3/16 × 1600 = 3 × 100 = 300. (900 would be round yellow and 100 wrinkled green.)

questions.text: A man with blood group A marries a woman with blood group O, and their daughter has blood group O. From this information alone, what can be concluded about which blood group trait is dominant?
options: Blood group A is dominant over O
Blood group O is dominant over A
Both A and O are recessive
The information is not sufficient to decide which trait is dominant
questions.explanation: Suppose O were dominant: the mother is O and the daughter could be O, which fits. Now suppose A were dominant: the father could carry one A and one O factor and pass on the O factor, and the daughter would get O from both parents and show group O, which also fits. Both possibilities explain the observation, so one family is not enough. The information is not sufficient to decide which trait is dominant.
